## What carries over

Goal: improve at 9x9 Go across fresh sessions, ultimately win consistently against human-style KataGo 9d.

## Record
- Game 1: Black vs 9d, Chinese area scoring, komi 7. Lost by resignation after White move 56 (D2).
- Game 2: White vs 4k, same rules. Lost by resignation after Black move 49 (J6). No captures or numerical final score.
- Read game-001.md for review. game-001.sgf is the full move record; game-001-log.json contains every returned position.
- Read game-002.md for the latest review; game-002.sgf and game-002-log.json contain the complete record.
- No successful level has been established. One loss does not establish individual move values.

## Lessons to use immediately
1. Count prospective area early, especially after about 10-16 moves. With all 81 points assigned, Black needs at least 45 for a win with 7 komi; 44-37 is a draw. If there is neutral area, compare actual totals instead.
2. Center influence must yield territory, an attack, or access to a viable invasion. Game 1 built a narrow central chain while White took both sides.
3. Check two eyes for every major group before treating it as safe. Connected stones and many present liberties are not proof of life. Preserve eye space and a base before filling internal points.
4. In capture reading, rebuild the position after each capture. Captured stones open liberties for adjacent enemy groups. The D8/E9 sacrifice in game 1 overlooked this.
5. Ko eyes are not unconditional eyes. Game 1's lower D2 and upper E8 spaces depended on vulnerable isolated Black stones. Owning two such ko positions does not by itself guarantee double-ko life.
6. Do not repeat the complete opening E5 C5 E3 D7 F7 G5 G6 H6 G7 G3 without reconsidering its territorial consequences. E5 itself was not shown to be wrong.
7. Game 2 counted an insecure right-side base as territory. Black G2 followed by H1 undermined the corner; J4/J5 occupied remaining eye space. The final seven-stone White right group had only H4 and J2 as liberties and a concrete forced-capture route. Connected second-line stones do not guarantee a base.
8. Use permitted current-board group/liberty inspection during contact fights. Game 2 missed that Black D3 put White D4/E4 in atari with only C4 available; White played J8 instead. Scan ALL own groups before pursuing a distant plan.
9. Before invading, identify two prospective eyes or a concrete escape/connection. Game 2's late G8/H7/J8 invasion had no demonstrated life; trapping H9 would provide only one prospective eye.
10. Check the opponent's simplest connection. In game 2, White E4 did not separate the lower Black stones: Black F4 joined F3 and F5 and squeezed White's right group.

- Choose a rank deliberately. Both 9d and 4k games were lost. 8k is a reasonable next practice experiment for territory and life, not an established best training rank. 9d remains the target.

- Before each move: identify atari/cuts, weakest group and eye prospects, largest area gain, and whether opponent can ignore the intended threat.

# Game 1: Black vs 9d — W+R

Played 2026-10-05. 9x9, Chinese area scoring, White komi 7, simple ko.
Black resigned after move 56, White D2. No numerical final score was produced.
The opponent was the strongest available human-style profile. This was a baseline, not a calibrated training level.

## Full record
- game-001.sgf: standard SGF, all 56 stone moves.
- game-001-log.json: tool responses including every board and final resignation.
- Final captures: Black 2, White 2. Final ko point: D1.

## Main strategic failure
Black occupied the center and connected many stones, but White obtained the left and right sides. Center influence did not become enough area or a productive attack. By the middle game, the rough territorial count was clearly losing even assuming the main Black chain survived.

The opening was:
1 B E5, 2 W C5, 3 B E3, 4 W D7, 5 B F7, 6 W G5,
7 B G6, 8 W H6, 9 B G7, 10 W G3, 11 B C3, 12 W C6.
Black's upper-right contact exchanges let White establish the right side. This is an observation about the resulting position, not proof that a particular opening move was objectively inferior. Earlier C3 or a more territorial response to G5 are candidates for future manual study.

## Concrete tactical error: the upper cut
31 B D8, 32 W C8 put D8 in atari.
33 B E9, 34 W D9 captured D8.
I had considered capturing E8 with F8, but overlooked that removing D8 opened a NEW liberty at D8 for White E8. E9 itself was also in atari after White D9, so 35 B F9 was needed to extend it.

Later, 49 B F8 put E8 in atari. White played 50 J7, allowing 51 B D8 to capture E8. This created a ko at E8 rather than a secure new eye: Black D8 had only E8 as a liberty.
The lesson is to account for liberties exposed by removed stones, and distinguish a ko capture from unconditional life.

## Life-and-death failure
The central chain had almost no internal eye space. At the end:
- G9 was a genuine enclosed eye point.
- D2 was an apparent lower eye whose border stone D1 was isolated and in atari after White E1.
- E8 was an apparent upper eye whose border stone D8 was isolated and in atari.
- Filling either D2 or E8 to connect the vulnerable stone would consume that eye space.

55 B J9 gained the corner point, but 56 W D2 captured D1 and started a ko at D1.
Black was already far behind in area and had no identified adequate ko threat to protect the lower eye. The main chain's life was therefore also in serious jeopardy. Resignation was appropriate.

Do not describe this as established double-ko seki. Both vulnerable appendages were initially Black stones; after White takes one ko, Black cannot automatically capture at the other, already-owned ko as a response.

## What worked, within limits
- 37 B D1 forced 38 W B1 and secured a useful boundary point at the time.
- 39 B G4 required 41 B E4 after White F3 put F4/G4 in atari.
- 43 B F6 forced 44 W H5.
- 53 B D6 forced 54 W C7.
These local gains did not repair the opening's area deficit or the global eye problem.

## Next experiment
Keep the first move flexible; E5 was not disproved. Prioritize territory and eye space sooner, count both sides before the board becomes crowded, and reconsider contact exchanges that merely give the opponent a safe side group. A lower-ranked practice opponent is an option, but no training rank has been calibrated yet.

No external analysis engine or automated move recommendation was used. The review is manual and its proposed alternatives are unverified.

# Game 2: White vs 4k — B+R

Played 2026-10-05. 9x9, Chinese area scoring, White komi 7, simple ko.
White resigned after move 49, Black J6. No numerical final score was produced.
4k was chosen as a territory-and-life training experiment after the game-1 loss against 9d. This loss does not establish a successful training rank.

## Full record
- game-002.sgf: all 49 stone moves, colors, opponent, rules, komi, result.
- game-002-log.json: every returned position and the resignation response.
- Final captures: Black 0, White 0. No ko occurred.

## Main failure: counting a base that did not exist
White began C3, C6, G3. The left-side framework was more territorial than game 1's central chain, but the lower-right group never secured two eyes. I counted prospective right-side area too generously and then treated extra connected stones as progress toward life.

Key sequence:
23 B G2, 24 W H2, 25 B F1, 26 W D2, 27 B H1, 28 W H3.
Black undercut the right group and occupied H1. White's H2/H3 connection did not secure the corner: H1 prevented J1 from functioning as an eye boundary. White should have re-evaluated the entire base at G2, and especially before playing elsewhere at move 26. Alternatives such as H3 instead of H2 need manual examination; this game does not establish their value.

37 B J4, 38 W J3, 39 B J5, 40 W G8.
The edge invasion occupied the remaining right-side eye space. The problem was already serious before J4; J4 was not merely a small territorial reduction. Starting another invasion did not rescue the first group.

42 W E4, 43 B F4.
I hoped E4 might separate the lower Black stones or help a connection. F4 connected F3 to F5 and removed a liberty of the right group. E4 did not force the intended separation.

At the final position, White G3/G4/G5/H2/H3/H5/J3 had exactly two liberties: H4 and J2.
Neither was an eye. Black H4 joins the large Black chain and leaves White J2 as its sole liberty. White J2 then exposes only J1; Black J1 captures the group. White cannot subsequently save it by J1: that fills its last liberty without capturing Black H1, which still has G1 available. Playing White H4 first likewise supplies no new liberty.
This is concrete local evidence for the group's failure, beyond a vague lack of eyes.

## Second invasion: too little room, too late
40 W G8, 41 B F8, 44 W H7, 45 B H9, 46 W G9, 48 W J8, 49 B J6.
White found a possible net against H9, but the three White components were still separate:
- G8/G9: liberties F9, G7, H8.
- H7: liberties G7, H8, J7.
- J8: liberties H8, J7, J9.

H8 would connect them and threaten H9. Capturing H9 would provide only one prospective eye; F9, G7, and J7 were boundary liberties that Black could contest. I had no demonstrated two-eye life or escape. A trapped enemy stone is not by itself a living invasion. The upper-right was not played out, so this review does not claim an engine-proven death.

## Missed immediate atari
47 B D3 left White D4/E4 with C4 as its ONLY liberty. I played 48 J8 without noticing this atari. C4 would connect D4/E4 to C3 and the main left group. It would not fix the overall loss, but ignoring a threatened two-stone group was a separate tactical mistake.

The final left group A5/B5/B6/C5/C6/D6/D7/E6/E7 had A4, B4, C4, C7 as liberties. Its access to the lower-left remained broad, but those liberties alone were not a proof of life. C3 and D2 were also separate stones, not a fully connected territorial boundary.

## What to carry forward
1. Run a current-board group/liberty inventory before moves in contact fights. This is allowed inspection, not move selection. In this game it would have exposed both the right group's shrinking liberties and D4/E4's atari.
2. Count unsecured side space separately from viable territory. A group lacking eyes or an escape must not contribute its whole surrounding region to an optimistic winning count.
3. Against an undercut, preserve the base before playing elsewhere. In particular, study the G2/H2/H1 sequence rather than assuming a connected second-line stone protects the corner.
4. Before invading, name the intended two eyes or a concrete connection route. The late upper-right invasion repeated the life problem in a smaller space.
5. Check the opponent's simplest connection: F4 joined F3 and F5. An adjacent attacking move does not force a cut.
6. A lower practice rank, for example 8k, is a reasonable next experiment to rehearse life and territory. It is not an established optimal rank; 9d remains the target.

All decisions and review were manual. Code only logged tool results, converted moves to SGF, and inspected the final board's groups and liberties. No engine, automated recommendations, or sequence-search program was used.

## Lessons to use immediately
1. Count prospective area early, especially after about 10-16 moves. With all 81 points assigned, Black needs at least 45 for a win with 7 komi; 44-37 is a draw. If there is neutral area, compare actual totals instead.
2. Center influence must yield territory, an attack, or access to a viable invasion. Game 1 built a narrow central chain while White took both sides.
3. Check two eyes for every major group before treating it as safe. Connected stones and many present liberties are not proof of life. Preserve eye space and a base before filling internal points.
4. In capture reading, rebuild the position after each capture. Captured stones open liberties for adjacent enemy groups. The D8/E9 sacrifice in game 1 overlooked this.
5. Ko eyes are not unconditional eyes. Game 1's lower D2 and upper E8 spaces depended on vulnerable isolated Black stones. Owning two such ko positions does not by itself guarantee double-ko life.
6. Do not repeat the complete opening E5 C5 E3 D7 F7 G5 G6 H6 G7 G3 without reconsidering its territorial consequences. E5 itself was not shown to be wrong.
7. Game 2 counted an insecure right-side base as territory. Black G2 followed by H1 undermined the corner; J4/J5 occupied remaining eye space. The final seven-stone White right group had only H4 and J2 as liberties and a concrete forced-capture route. Connected second-line stones do not guarantee a base.
8. Use permitted current-board group/liberty inspection during contact fights. Game 2 missed that Black D3 put White D4/E4 in atari with only C4 available; White played J8 instead. Scan ALL own groups before pursuing a distant plan.
9. Before invading, identify two prospective eyes or a concrete escape/connection. Game 2's late G8/H7/J8 invasion had no demonstrated life; trapping H9 would provide only one prospective eye.
10. Check the opponent's simplest connection. In game 2, White E4 did not separate the lower Black stones: Black F4 joined F3 and F5 and squeezed White's right group.
11. Three connected empty edge points are not already two eyes. In game 3, White J8 occupied the middle of J7/J8/J9. Black J7, White J5 left the seven-stone upper-right group with only J9. Black J9 would capture J8 but leave the entire eight-stone group with only J8; White J8 captures it all. This is not ko. Simply substituting J8 for J6 at move 61 was not verified to save it: J6 also needed boundary protection.
12. Check the hane's cut and the new stone's own liberties. Game 3's A5 was left in atari by White B5; A6 was suicide. White A6 later captured A5 and reopened A5 for the neighboring White edge group. Black A1 then had only B1, and White B1 captured it, reopening A1. Both planned edge squeezes ignored liberties opened by captures.
13. An invasion can gain connected stones without gaining a base. Game 3's C8/D8/D7/C7/B7/D9 ended with only B8 and C9 as liberties. White A8/A7 and E9 denied eye boundaries. The later upper-right entry also failed; neither upper group was saved.

## Next-game focus
- Choose a rank deliberately. Games against 9d, 4k and 8k were lost. Consider 12k next to practise basic tactical reading and eyes; it is an experiment, not an established best training rank. 9d remains the target.
- Keep opening alternatives as hypotheses. Securing a corner/lower-side position earlier (for example considering C3 before the upper-right exchanges) is worth trying, not established as best.
- Before each move: identify atari/cuts, weakest group and eye prospects, largest area gain, and whether opponent can ignore the intended threat.
- In contact fights, inspect current-board groups/liberties before EVERY move. In game 3 inspection was useful but intermittent; detecting danger after losing eye space was too late.
- Name eye boundaries and the required dividing move before calling a group safe. Preserve both corner boundaries and outside liberties; an invading stone's capture may still leave only one eye.
- Count secure area and unsecured potential separately. Re-evaluate the base immediately after an undercut; do not defer it merely because the group has present liberties.
- Save complete move records, final result, and a small number of concrete lessons after each game. Update this file with the latest record and evidence.
